title: Lane Position & Space
summary: How to pick your spot in the lane, keep a space cushion around you, and use the SEE strategy to stay ahead of hazards.

sections.heading: Your space cushion and three lane paths

blocks.text: Keep a cushion of space between you and other vehicles. It gives you a clear view of traffic, and if someone makes a mistake, you have more time to respond and more space to maneuver, including an escape path.
Each traffic lane gives a motorcycle three paths of travel: path 1 is the left third, path 2 is the center, and path 3 is the right third. Choose a position that helps you:

items: See and be seen.
Stay out of other drivers' blind spots.
Avoid surface hazards.
Communicate what you plan to do.
Avoid windblast from other vehicles.
Keep an escape path open.
Set up for turns.

blocks.text: Many riders treat the left third as their default, but change position as conditions change. No part of the lane has to be avoided, including the center.

Oil drippings and debris collect in the center third of the lane. Unless the road is wet, this strip still gives adequate traction. You can also ride just left or right of the grease strip and stay in the center third.

items: Avoid big buildups of oil and grease, usually found at busy intersections and tollbooths.

blocks.text: Experienced riders use their own judgment about lane position, with one absolute rule: never ride in another vehicle's blind spot.

Following too closely is a frequent factor in motorcycle crashes. In traffic, a motorcycle needs as much distance to stop as a car. Keep at least two seconds behind the vehicle ahead under normal conditions.

items: Pick a marker on or near the road ahead, such as a lamppost or pavement marking.
When the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, count "one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two."
If you reach the marker before you say "two," you are following too closely.

blocks.text: Two seconds gives you the minimum room to stop or swerve if the driver ahead stops suddenly. It also gives you a better view of potholes and other road hazards.
Open up three seconds or more when:

items: The pavement is slippery.
You cannot see through the vehicle ahead (like a van or truck).
Traffic is heavy and someone may squeeze in front of you.
Your motorcycle will take longer than normal to stop.

blocks.text: Stay well back even when stopped. That space lets you escape if a driver behind you does not stop, and gives you a cushion if the vehicle ahead backs up.

Behind a car, ride where the driver can see you in the inside rearview mirror. The center of the lane usually puts you there. Drivers check the inside mirror far more often than their sideview mirrors.
If someone is tailgating you, do not speed up. You may just end up being tailgated at a higher speed. Instead, get them in front of you:

items: Let them pass.
If they cannot pass, slow down and open up extra space ahead so you both have room to stop. This also encourages them to pass.
You can also turn off the road, or pull into a parking area, and re-enter later.

blocks.text: To pass another vehicle:

items: Ride in the left portion of your lane at a safe following distance, so you can see farther and be seen. Signal, check for oncoming traffic, use your mirrors and turn your head to check your blind spot.
When it is safe, move into the left lane and accelerate. Pick a position that does not crowd the car and leaves space to avoid hazards in your lane.
Do not linger in the other vehicle's blind spot.
Signal again, do mirror and head checks before returning to your lane, then cancel the signal.

blocks.text: Complete every pass within the posted speed limit, and pass only where it is permitted. Know your signs and roadway markings.
When you are being passed, stay in the center portion of your lane. Riding close to the passing vehicle is risky because of:

items: A small mistake by either of you, which could cause a sideswipe.
Extended mirrors. Some drivers forget their mirrors stick out past their fenders.
Objects thrown from windows. A passenger may not see you even if the driver does.
Wind blasts from larger vehicles, which can affect your control. Being in the farther part of your lane gives you more room for error.

sections.heading: Lane sharing, merging and riding alongside

blocks.text: Cars and motorcycles each need a full lane to operate safely, and the manual notes that lane sharing is usually prohibited. Riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane leaves you exposed: a hand could come out a window, a door could open, or a car could turn suddenly. Check your state's rule in the State Cheat Sheet.
Discourage others from squeezing past you by keeping a center-portion position. Drivers are most tempted to do this:

items: In heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic.
When they want to pass you.
When you are getting ready to turn at an intersection.
When you are moving into an exit lane or leaving a highway.

blocks.text: Drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you. Give them plenty of room: change lanes if one is open, or adjust your speed to open up space for the merging vehicle.

Avoid riding next to cars or trucks in other lanes. You may be in their blind spot, and they could move into your lane. They also block your escape if trouble appears ahead. Speed up or drop back to a spot that is clear on both sides.
SEE stands for Search, Evaluate, Execute. It helps you read traffic and plan and carry out the safest action.

rows: Scan ahead, to the sides and behind. Look especially for escape paths around intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones.
Think about how hazards could combine to create risk: road surfaces, traffic signals and signs, and vehicles that may move into your path. Have a plan.
Act smoothly: communicate with your lights and/or horn, adjust your speed, and adjust your position or direction.

blocks.text: When searching, think in three time zones:

rows: Your immediate, urgent path. Enough time and space to swerve and/or brake.
How far ahead to search, so you can prepare before a situation becomes urgent

items: Two hazards: take them one at a time. Adjust your speed so they separate, then deal with each as a single hazard.
Three or more hazards: decisions get harder. Weigh the consequences of each and give equal distance to the hazards.

blocks.text: In high-risk areas such as intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones, cover the clutch and both brakes. This cuts the time you need to react.

keyPoints: A space cushion gives you time to respond and room to maneuver, including an escape path.
Each lane has three paths; move away from hazards and use the center (path 2) when traffic is on both sides.
The one absolute rule: never ride in another vehicle's blind spot.
Keep at least 2 seconds of following distance, and 3 or more when slippery, when you cannot see past the vehicle ahead, or in heavy traffic.
Ride where drivers ahead can see you in their inside mirror, usually the center of the lane.
Let tailgaters pass; if they cannot, slow down and add space ahead instead of speeding up.
When being passed, or when drivers might squeeze by, hold a center-portion position.
Use SEE (Search, Evaluate, Execute): search 12 seconds ahead and treat anything within 4 seconds as urgent.
